insets.text: TEMPORARY PLACEMENT  —  BRINDLEWICK COMMUNITY CLINIC  —  FOUR WEEKS

arrival.text:
By the time the bus sighs into Brindlewick, the sea has gone the color of pewter and every window on the hill is catching the last light.

You have come for a temporary work assignment: records cleanup, patient scheduling, a little triage support if the clinic gets busy. Practical work. Necessary work. The kind of work you understand.

Then you notice the lanterns.

Small ones. Blue glass, green glass, plain jam jars with tea lights inside. They sit in windows all along the harbor road, unlit in the daylight, waiting.

overlays.text: A town can look ordinary until it notices you noticing it.

choices.label: Head to the inn and get settled.
Pause by the harbor windows and study the lanterns.

insets.text: TAG ON A BLUE LANTERN  —  FOR ANYONE COMING HOME LATE

first_lantern.text:
The nearest lantern hangs behind the bakery window, tied with thread and a paper tag gone soft at the edges. There is no flame inside it, but when your shadow crosses the glass, the wick gives off one brief pinprick of light.

A boy of maybe twelve watches you from the bakery step, a paper bag of rolls hugged against his coat.

"You're new," he says. "New people always stare at the lanterns like they're going to blink first."

choices.label: Ask him what the lanterns are for.
Smile, thank him, and continue to the inn.

meet_nico.text:
"Lantern Rounds," the boy says, as if that explains everything.

When it clearly doesn't, he shifts the bag of rolls and tries again. "On certain nights, people leave lanterns in windows for anyone who's lost. Not just lost-lost. Sad lost. Waiting lost. Forgot-where-you-belong lost. My gran says the lanterns remember the way when people can't."

He looks briefly embarrassed by how much he believes it.

"I'm Nico. If Mrs. Vale at the inn asks, I absolutely did not spend the bakery change on ginger biscuits."

overlays.text: Forgot-where-you-belong lost.

choices.label: Promise not to betray him to Mrs. Vale.
Tell him secrets are expensive in a town this small.

insets.text: GUEST REGISTER  —  ROOM 3  —  ELISE MARLOW  —  TEMPORARY
A ginger biscuit appears beside your key without comment.

harbor_inn.text:
The Salt Finch Inn smells of lemon oil, rain wool, and bread warming somewhere behind a closed door. Its owner, Mara Vale, is small, elderly, and composed in the way of people who have survived enough storms to stop flinching at weather.

"Clinic sent word," she says, sliding a brass key across the counter. "Room three. Radiator complains, but it works. Breakfast at seven unless the harbor fog gets dramatic. It does enjoy an audience."

Behind her, on the sill, stands a lantern made from green glass. Its tag is turned inward.

overlays.text: The lantern in the inn window feels less like decoration than a held breath.

choices.label: Ask Mrs. Vale about the green lantern.
Leave the subject alone and prepare for your first clinic shift.

vale_lantern.text:
Mrs. Vale's eyes move to the sill. For a moment she looks older than she did a breath ago.

"Every house keeps one if it wants to," she says. "For travelers. For the lonely. For those who left a sentence unfinished. Brindlewick has always been sentimental about sentences."

You ask whose sentence the green lantern is keeping.

Her hand rests on the register, covering an old ink stain shaped like a thumbprint.

"A friend," she says. "Liora Wren. She vanished seventeen years ago on Lantern Night. Half the town remembers her as a tragedy. The other half remembers her as an argument."

overlays.text: A friend. A tragedy. An argument.

choices.label: Gently ask what Mrs. Vale believes happened.
Decide not to press her tonight.

insets.text: HANDWRITTEN NOTE, FOUND TUCKED UNDER THE GREEN LANTERN  —  M., KEEP IT LIT ONLY IF SOMEONE ASKS KINDLY.

vale_memory.text:
Mrs. Vale opens a drawer and removes a folded note, creased nearly soft enough to tear.

"Liora was our district nurse before there was a clinic worth naming. She delivered babies in kitchens, sat with old men who pretended they weren't afraid, and remembered everybody's tea the way some people remember birthdays."

She gives you the note, but not quite into your hand.

"She also knew when people were lying to themselves. Brindlewick did not always thank her for that."

choices.label: Read the note carefully.
Tell Mrs. Vale she can keep it private.

insets.text: APPOINTMENT NOTES  —  08:10 CHECK-IN  —  09:00 RECORDS ROOM  —  11:30 HOME VISIT SUPPORT

clinic_morning.text:
The clinic is smaller than the assignment brief implied: two exam rooms, a waiting area full of mismatched chairs, and a records room that seems to contain every paper the town has ever been afraid to throw away.

A tired woman in navy scrubs introduces herself as Tessa Rowe. Nurse, scheduler, driver when the roads flood, and, apparently, the only person who knows which cabinet has stopped locking.

"You'll hear things," Tessa says, handing you a stack of folders. "People talk around strangers. Sometimes that's useful. Sometimes it's just lonely."

overlays.text: She has the worn patience of someone who keeps showing up after everyone else goes home.

choices.label: Offer to help Tessa with the home visits after records work.
Focus on the archived records about Lantern Night.

insets.text: HOME VISIT LOG  —  ROWE, T.  —  THREE STOPS  —  WEATHER: FOG BANK RISING

home_visits.text:
By noon, you have carried prescriptions up three steep lanes, repaired a kettle plug with tape that will not hold, and listened to a retired fisherman describe the exact sound fog makes when it is thinking about becoming rain.

At the final cottage, an old woman grips your wrist with papery strength.

"Liora came here the night she vanished," she says. "Not for me. For the baby in the lighthouse house. People forget that part because grief prefers simpler shapes."

Tessa goes still beside you.

overlays.text: People forget that part because grief prefers simpler shapes.

choices.label: Ask Tessa what she knows about the lighthouse house.
Make sure the old woman is comfortable before asking anything else.

insets.text: OLD CLINIC LEDGER  —  L. WREN  —  LAST ENTRY: LANTERN NIGHT, 17 YEARS AGO
Mara Vale's initials appear in the margin beside the final entry.

records_room.text:
The records room has its own weather: dust, paper, and the dry hush of things not ready to be found.

Liora Wren's handwriting is neat until the final page, where it slants sharply across the ledger.

Emergency call. Lighthouse house. Child fevered. Caleb's boat delayed. Mayor insists Lantern Rounds cancelled due to storm. Will go anyway.

Below that, someone has written in pencil: She always went anyway.

overlays.text: She always went anyway.

choices.label: Copy the ledger entry before anyone can remove it.
Bring the ledger straight to Tessa.

insets.text: TEA BAG TAG  —  BREATHE FIRST. DECIDE SECOND.

tessa_confides.text:
Tessa makes tea strong enough to qualify as infrastructure.

"My mother trained under Liora," she says. "Everyone thinks Liora vanished because she was reckless, or heartbroken, or touched by some old superstition. But my mother said Liora was carrying something that night. Not a secret exactly. Proof."

She rubs both hands over her face.

"Councilman Orret wants the Lantern Rounds stopped this year. Says they're unhealthy. Says the town keeps rehearsing grief. Some days I think he's right. Then someone leaves a lantern for a widow or a new baby or a stranger in room three, and I don't know."

overlays.text: A stranger in room three.

choices.label: Say traditions can hurt and still be worth understanding.
Say the truth matters more than keeping people comfortable.
Say people need gentleness before answers.

insets.text: PUBLIC NOTICE  —  PROPOSAL TO SUSPEND THE LANTERN ROUNDS  —  HEARING TONIGHT

council_notice.text:
The notice is posted crookedly on the town hall door. Someone has tried to smooth the paper. Someone else has drawn a small lantern in the corner.

Councilman Orret stands beneath it with a folder under one arm, talking to a reporter from the mainland. He has the careful voice of a man who has practiced sounding reasonable.

"Brindlewick deserves to move forward," he says. "Not remain trapped in a ritual built around a disappearance no one can explain."

choices.label: Introduce yourself and ask why he wants the tradition stopped now.
Avoid the crowd and look for Nico.
Return to the clinic and compare the notice with old records.

orret_confrontation.text:
Orret turns to you with polite suspicion.

"Temporary clinic staff," he says. "Yes, I've heard. Then you have an advantage. You can leave. The rest of us have to live with the consequences of people treating grief like civic duty."

You ask about Liora Wren.

For the first time, his voice loses polish.

"Liora was kind," he says. "People mistake that for harmless. It is not harmless, being kind in public. It makes cowards visible."

overlays.text: It is not harmless, being kind in public.

choices.label: Press him about the cancelled Lantern Rounds.
Let him keep his dignity and listen for what he does not say.

insets.text: TOWN RECORD EXCERPT  —  LANTERN NIGHT STORM CLOSURE  —  SIGNED: A. ORRET, ACTING HARBOR WARDEN

orret_slip.text:
"The storm closure saved lives," Orret says. "Roads washed out. Boats lost sight of shore. Someone had to make a hard decision."

"But Liora went anyway," you say.

His jaw tightens.

"Liora had a habit of believing one person mattered more than the rules meant to protect everyone."

A gull cries above the hall, sharp as tearing paper.

choices.label: Ask whether the child at the lighthouse survived.
Take the question to the old town records instead.

insets.text: NICO'S MAP  —  STARS, TIDE MARKS, AND ONE VERY DRAMATIC SKULL THAT HE INSISTS IS A ROCK

nico_map.text:
Nico is at the breakwater, chalking lantern shapes onto flat stones. He has drawn the town as a spiral: inn, clinic, town hall, lighthouse, and an empty place at the center labeled DON'T ASK MRS. VALE UNLESS SHE'S HAD TEA.

"The lanterns don't just remember sad things," he says. "They remember when somebody came back. People forget that part. Adults love forgetting the useful bits."

He points to the lighthouse.

"There's a box under the old fog bell. My gran said Liora left it for someone who would ask the right question."

overlays.text: You kept Nico's harmless secret. He offers you a real one.

choices.label: Go to the lighthouse before the hearing.
Ask Nico to bring Mrs. Vale to the hearing later.

insets.text: ARCHIVE INDEX  —  HARBOR CLOSURES, BIRTH REGISTERS, CHARITABLE FUND LEDGERS
The name Caleb appears beside three unpaid fuel bills and one receipt for a green glass lantern.

records_return.text:
The archive lives in the back of the library, where the air is cool and the radiator mutters like an old judge.

You find the storm closure order. You find the birth register for a child at the lighthouse house. You find a charitable fund created one week after Liora vanished, signed by Orret, Vale, and Rowe.

Not hush money. Not exactly.

A promise, maybe. A way to keep someone housed, fed, forgiven.

overlays.text: Grief prefers simpler shapes.

choices.label: Follow the records toward the lighthouse.
Bring what you found to Mrs. Vale first.

insets.text: GREEN LANTERN TAG, TURNED OUTWARD AT LAST  —  FOR LIORA, WHO WENT ANYWAY

vale_confession.text:
Mrs. Vale reads the copies without sitting down.

"We told ourselves we were protecting the child," she says. "Protecting Liora's memory. Protecting Orret from the kind of shame that makes men crueler than they began. It was easier to make a tradition than tell the story straight."

Her hand trembles against the counter.

"Liora didn't vanish because the lanterns took her. She vanished because she saved a child in a storm, got the mother to shelter, then went back for Caleb when his boat light failed. The sea kept him. The road kept her. We found her coat three days later. No body. No goodbye."

overlays.text: No body. No goodbye. A town can build a whole ritual around an unfinished sentence.

choices.label: Ask Mrs. Vale to come with you to the lighthouse.
Promise to handle the truth carefully.

insets.text: WEATHER ADVISORY  —  FOG AFTER SUNSET  —  TIDE TURNING 19:40

lighthouse_path.text:
The lighthouse road climbs away from town through grass silvered by salt. Below, Brindlewick begins lighting its windows one by one.

A lantern appears in the clinic. Another in the bakery. Another in the inn.

The road bends at the old fog bell. Beneath it, half-hidden by sea thrift and rust, is a small wooden box sealed with oilcloth.

overlays.text: The town is not watching you. It is waiting with you.
Breathe first. Decide second.

choices.label: Open the box.
Wait until someone from town arrives.

insets.text: LETTER, OILCLOTH-WRAPPED  —  IF THIS IS FOUND, PLEASE DO NOT MAKE ME BRAVER THAN I WAS
Inside the box: a letter, a cracked lantern lens, and a clinic badge with Liora Wren's name worn almost smooth.

liora_box.text:
The letter is written in Liora's hand.

She explains that the storm closure was necessary. She explains that she broke it anyway because a child was fevered, because a mother was frightened, because Caleb had gone out to fetch medicine from a boat that should never have left harbor.

Then the handwriting changes, rushed by weather or fear.

If I do not come home, tell them this: nobody is a lesson. Not me. Not Caleb. Not the child. Leave a light for the next person, not for the story you prefer.

overlays.text: Nobody is a lesson.

choices.label: Take the letter to the hearing and reveal it plainly.
Carry the letter back with care and ask the town to hear it together.
Keep the letter private for Mrs. Vale and Tessa.

insets.text: PRIVATE NOTE  —  LIORA'S LETTER PLACED IN CLINIC SAFE  —  WITNESSES: E. MARLOW, T. ROWE

quiet_room.text:
You bring the letter to Tessa. Mrs. Vale arrives soon after, rain on her shoulders, Nico hovering at the doorway until someone pretends not to see him listening.

They read it in silence.

No one is healed by a page. But something in the room changes shape. The story is no longer only fog, road, and absence. It has Liora's own words in it now, asking not to be polished into a symbol.

choices.label: Go to the hearing with them, even if you do not reveal everything.
Let the town keep its old story tonight.

insets.text: PUBLIC HEARING  —  ATTENDANCE: STANDING ROOM ONLY
Mrs. Vale stands near the back, green lantern in both hands.
Tessa has not sat down once. She keeps watching the door, as if ready to leave for whoever needs her next.

hearing.text:
The town hall is full of damp coats, low voices, and lantern light trembling in jars along the windowsills.

Orret speaks first. He does not sound triumphant. He sounds tired.

"We have mistaken repetition for remembrance," he says. "Tonight I ask that we end the Lantern Rounds. Not because Liora Wren should be forgotten, but because we have used her absence to avoid our own lives."

Every face turns when you stand.

overlays.text: Leave a light for the next person, not for the story you prefer.

choices.label: Read Liora's letter aloud and let the town hear the whole truth.
Invite Mrs. Vale, Tessa, and Orret to tell the story together.
Argue that some traditions must end before people can heal.
Let the room decide without you.

town_response.text:
For a long moment after you finish, the hall is so quiet you can hear rain ticking at the roof.

Then Mrs. Vale steps forward. Tessa follows. To your surprise, Orret does too.

The story comes out unevenly: storm, fever, boat light, road washout, fear, pride, kindness, all the human pieces that never fit cleanly into one version. People cry. Some look angry. Some look relieved to have a shape for what they inherited.

At the windows, every lantern flame leans toward the glass.

overlays.text: The lanterns remember care. Not just grief. Care.
You did not arrive belonging here. You arrived paying attention.

choices.label: Help the town remake the Lantern Rounds around the living.
Preserve the tradition, but give Liora back her real name.
Support ending the Lantern Rounds with honesty.
Extinguish the green lantern.

insets.text: NEW LANTERN TAGS  —  FOR THE LOST  —  FOR THE FOUND  —  FOR THE ONES STILL ON THEIR WAY
Nico's first official tag reads: FOR PEOPLE WHO PRETEND THEY DON'T NEED BISCUITS.

good_renewal.text:
By morning, nobody agrees on exactly what happened at the hearing. That feels honest.

The Lantern Rounds do not end. They change.

Some lanterns are lit for Liora. Some for Caleb. Some for people still living, which turns out to be harder and more necessary. The clinic starts a visiting list. The inn keeps a spare room fund. Orret resigns from the harbor committee but stays to stack chairs after meetings.

Your temporary placement remains temporary. Still, when your bus comes, Mrs. Vale presses a small blue lantern into your hands.

"For wherever you are between places," she says.

On the ride out, you look back and see Brindlewick shining in the gray morning: not fixed, not finished, but lit.

overlays.text: Every choice leaves a mark. Some marks become windows.

insets.text: ARCHIVE ADDENDUM  —  LIORA WREN RECORD AMENDED  —  CAUSE: LOST DURING STORM RESPONSE

bittersweet_good.text:
The town does not transform all at once. No town does.

But Liora's letter is copied into the archive. The clinic ledger is corrected. The green lantern moves from Mrs. Vale's private sill to the town hall, where anyone can read the tag beneath it.

The Lantern Rounds continue for one final year, not as performance, but as farewell. People light windows for the missing, the lonely, and the living they have neglected to call.

When you leave Brindlewick, Tessa hugs you with exhausted strength. Mrs. Vale does not cry until she thinks you are no longer looking.

You do not belong to the town. But some part of you will always know the road back.

overlays.text: Leave a light for the next person.

insets.text: DEPARTURE  —  07:15  —  BRINDLEWICK TO NORTH STATION

neutral_unresolved.text:
You leave before the town decides what it can bear.

Maybe that is cowardice. Maybe it is respect. Maybe temporary people should not mistake access for wisdom.

From the bus window, Brindlewick looks peaceful. Lanterns still glow in a few windows, though daylight has already thinned them. Mrs. Vale's green one is among them.

Weeks later, a postcard arrives with no return address. On the front is the lighthouse. On the back, one sentence:

We are still talking.

You pin it above your desk and find that, on difficult evenings, you are glad they are.

overlays.text: Some mysteries do not close. They become invitations left ajar.

insets.text: GREEN LANTERN  —  EXTINGUISHED

lonely_bad.text:
You put out the green lantern because, in the moment, it feels like mercy.

The room exhales. Or maybe it only goes quiet.

Afterward, people leave without meeting one another's eyes. Mrs. Vale takes the lantern home wrapped in her coat. Tessa thanks you politely and does not ask for your help again. Nico watches from the doorway with an expression too old for his face.

The Lantern Rounds are suspended by morning.

Nothing terrible happens. That is almost worse. The town simply grows more efficient at being alone.

When your assignment ends, no one comes to see off the bus. As Brindlewick recedes behind rain-streaked glass, you tell yourself some lights need to go out.

You almost believe it.

overlays.text: Forgot-where-you-belong lost.
